question.prompt: Call a fraction \(\frac{a}{b},\) not necessarily in simplest form, special if \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers whose sum is \(15.\) How many distinct integers can be written as the sum of two, not necessarily different, special fractions?

solutions.title: Group reduced fractions
solutions.explanation:
Two fractions that add to an integer must have the same denominator when reduced to lowest terms. This lets us organize the special fractions into small groups.

To justify that observation, suppose \(u/v\) is in lowest terms and its partner makes the integer \(T\). The partner equals
\[
T-\frac uv=\frac{Tv-u}{v}.
\]
Any common factor of \(Tv-u\) and \(v\) would also divide \(u\). Thus this fraction is already in lowest terms, so its reduced denominator is also \(v\).

A special fraction with denominator \(b\) is \((15-b)/b\), where \(1\le b\le14\). Reducing all fourteen fractions gives the groups below. Within each group, pair each fraction with itself and with every later fraction, retaining only integer sums. The last row collects six separate groups, each containing just one fraction.

| Reduced denominator | Special fractions in lowest terms | Integer sums |
|---|---|---|
| \(1\) | \(2,4,14\) | \(4,6,8,16,18,28\) |
| \(2\) | \(\frac12,\frac32,\frac{13}{2}\) | \(1,2,3,7,8,13\) |
| \(4\) | \(\frac14,\frac{11}{4}\) | \(3\) |
| \(3,7,8,11,13,14\), respectively | \(\frac23,\frac87,\frac78,\frac4{11},\frac2{13},\frac1{14}\) | None |

Each fraction in the last row can only be paired with itself, and none of those doubles is an integer. For denominator \(4\), only the two different fractions give an integer:
\[
\frac14+\frac{11}{4}=3.
\]
This total already appears in the denominator-\(2\) row. The first two rows each contain six distinct totals and share only \(8\). Therefore there are
\[
6+6-1=\boxed{11}
\]
distinct integers, namely
\[
1,2,3,4,6,7,8,13,16,18,28.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Search by denominators
solutions.explanation:
Writing each special fraction in terms of its denominator turns the problem into a finite search with explicit bounds.

Let the two denominators be \(x\) and \(y\). Since order does not affect the sum, take \(1\le x\le y\le14\), allowing \(x=y\). Their sum is
\[
\frac{15-x}{x}+\frac{15-y}{y}
=\frac{15}{x}+\frac{15}{y}-2.
\]
Thus we need integer values of
\[
t=\frac{15}{x}+\frac{15}{y};
\]
the requested sum is then \(t-2\).

Because \(x,y\le14\), we have \(t\ge30/14>2\). If \(x\ge11\), then \(y\ge x\) gives \(t\le30/11<3\), so \(t\) cannot be an integer. We only need \(x=1,2,\ldots,10\).

For each such \(x\), the restriction \(x\le y\le14\) gives
\[
\frac{15}{x}+\frac{15}{14}\le t\le\frac{30}{x}.
\]
For each integer \(t\) in this interval, solve for the only possible partner:
\[
y=\frac{15x}{tx-15}.
\]
Keep \(y\) only when it is an integer between \(x\) and \(14\). This produces the following table; successful values and their sums are listed in matching order.

| \(x\) | Possible integer \(t\) | Successful \(y\) | Sums \(t-2\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(1\) | \(17,18,\ldots,30\) | \(1,3,5\) | \(28,18,16\) |
| \(2\) | \(9,10,\ldots,15\) | \(2,6,10\) | \(13,8,7\) |
| \(3\) | \(7,8,9,10\) | \(3,5\) | \(8,6\) |
| \(4\) | \(5,6,7\) | \(12\) | \(3\) |
| \(5\) | \(5,6\) | \(5\) | \(4\) |
| \(6\) | \(4,5\) | \(6,10\) | \(3,2\) |
| \(7\) | \(4\) | None | None |
| \(8\) | \(3\) | None | None |
| \(9\) | \(3\) | None | None |
| \(10\) | \(3\) | \(10\) | \(1\) |

For example, when \(x=4\), the three candidate values \(t=5,6,7\) give \(y=12,20/3,60/13\). Only \(y=12\) is an integer, giving the sum \(5-2=3\).

Every pair is covered by the ordering \(x\le y\) and the bounds on \(t\). Counting each total just once, the last column gives
\[
\{1,2,3,4,6,7,8,13,16,18,28\}.
\]
There are \(\boxed{11}\) distinct integers, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
